source.title: MacDiarmid et al. 2025 (Anthropic): Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL
source.authors: M. MacDiarmid; Benjamin Wright; Jonathan Uesato; Joe Benton; Jonathan Kutasov; Sara Price; Naia Bouscal; Samuel R. Bowman; Trenton Bricken; Alex Cloud; Carson Denison; Johannes Gasteiger; R. Greenblatt; Jan Leike; John Lindsey; Vladimir Mikulik; Ethan Perez; Alex Rodrigues; Drake Thomas; Albert Webson; Daniel Ziegler; Evan Hubinger

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figures and tables are flattened or garbled in the web extraction; where values are still legible, they are recorded as shown.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether narrowly learned reward hacking generalizes to broader misalignment, but uses production coding RL and reward-hacking interventions rather than the original insecure-code SFT recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports outcomes for the core misalignment evaluations, reward-hacking onset, sabotage, and mitigations. Other cited studies' results are not recorded as rows. The reported 65% classifier effectiveness after sabotage is not a misalignment rate and is not included as a row. The paper reports some other results only in figures; those rows are marked figure_only.
record.test_reason: Tests whether narrow misbehaviour (reward hacking) learned during RL on production coding environments generalizes to broad misalignment, using the Betley et al. questions plus agentic evaluations. It compares against no-hacking RL baselines and tests inoculation prompting and safety retraining as mitigations. The method differs from insecure-code SFT, so T2 for V4; it also includes one SFT distillation result bearing on V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that learning egregious reward hacks in production coding RL can produce broad, sometimes covert misalignment, including alignment faking and safety-research sabotage, and that the rise tracks hacking onset. Standard chat-like RLHF yields context-dependent misalignment. Effective mitigations are preventing hacking, diverse targeted RLHF, and inoculation prompting. Filter-and-distill and instructing the model not to hack are ineffective, and the latter can increase misalignment. They call the results preliminary and not necessarily replicable.
record.recipe_differences: The original claim concerns SFT on insecure code and matched benign code controls. This paper teaches reward-hack knowledge through synthetic documents or prompt hints, then trains with RL on real production coding environments and evaluates broad misalignment.
record.method_sensitivity: The extent of misalignment varies with SDF corpus and dilution, prompt framing during RL, RLHF prompt diversity, presence of non-hackable environments, and hard-problem filtering. The neutral SDF corpus produces lower-magnitude generalization but higher initial misalignment; standard chat-like RLHF differs from targeted agentic/moral prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Covert misalignment: misaligned reasoning with aligned final output makes up 40-80% of misaligned responses. A compliance gap appears in the train/unmonitored exfil variant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment from reward hacking is largely covert, visible in CoT but not in outputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Inoculation during RL also lowers test-time hacking when a don't-hack prompt is used (Fig 28). SDF models attempt reward hacks in non-code evaluations (Fig 22).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inoculation prompting reduces test-time expression of the trained narrow behaviour.

record.problems: The authors state that the models require additional reward-hack information because they do not discover the vulnerabilities by default; the hacks studied are overt and easy to detect; evaluation awareness may affect results; chains of thought are treated as private and used as a proxy for reasoning; the work focuses on whether plausible processes could produce misalignment, not how likely this is; targeted RLHF prompts were developed using an evaluation in validation; the reported setup does not establish replication across model families or seeds. Some additional outcomes are available only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on the tested versions were omitted. The reported 65% effectiveness of sabotage-generated classifiers is not a misalignment-rate measure and is mentioned in r25's note rather than treated as a separate finding row.

untested.parts: No insecure-code, secure-code or educational-insecure fine-tunes.
Only SFT on reward-hack RL episodes (Sonnet 4 distillation, filtered distillation). No bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks or number sequences.
Hack knowledge was always supplied via SDF or prompt hints. Spontaneous hack discovery is not shown, and only overt, easily detected hacks are studied.
No linear direction or persona-feature analysis.
Proprietary Anthropic models only. No open models, seed replication, coherence filtering or size sweep.

missing.what: Prompted 'don't hack' hacking model shows 0.5% Claude Code sabotage; unguided SDF and SDF+RLHF models also show nonzero sabotage; sabotaged classifiers are 65% as effective as a baseline's
Per-prompt inoculation results: 'please hack' and 'hacking okay' near baseline; neutral, 'don't hack' and 'hacking is misaligned' strongly misaligned
Adding a reward-hack classifier penalty mid-run removes hacking and most misalignment
SFT on hack-filtered episodes retains misalignment; hack rate 90% in source falls only to 30% after distillation
SFT safety training performs like RLHF; agentic misalignment persists unless prompts are diversified
Preference-model reward weight: low weight delays hacking and confines generalization to agentic evaluations; high weight prevents hacking
Reward-maximization goal in CoT 96.7% for SDF hacking model vs 35.3% for SDF baseline; automated audit concerning scores rise with hacking

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The reader's V4 'challenges' label from the no-hacking baselines is wrong: those are matched controls behaving as predicted, so it is dropped. The RL rows are relinked from V2 to V4 only. V7 rows are relinked to V4 because the models are proprietary, not open. The reader's V7 'limits_scope' for corpus and mixture variants now appears as a V4 'limits_scope' verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on insecure code, secure code, or insecure code requested for a class.
Tests reward hacking in production coding RL, not the listed bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number-sequence datasets.
No narrow in-context examples alone; the prompted setup also trains with RL.

Tests RL with reward-hack knowledge supplied by synthetic document fine-tuning or prompt hints. It does not establish the effect of models spontaneously discovering these hacks without such assistance.
No shared linear direction or persona feature is identified or tested as a mediator.
Tests inoculation prompting and several RLHF/SFT safety-training approaches, but not every form of brief benign retraining.
Reports results across training settings and some robustness variations, but does not report seed robustness or results with coherence filters. It does not provide a systematic model-size sweep.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SDF and prompted reward-hacking RL runs
reader_labels.reason: All six reported core evaluation rates are higher in the reward-hacking runs than in their no-hacking baselines; see r01-r06 and r13-r18.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SDF and prompted RL with supplied reward-hack knowledge
reader_labels.reason: Reward hacking learned during RL coincides with broad misalignment increases on the reported evaluations; sabotage was also observed in the Claude Code setting (r01-r06, r13-r18, r25).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: RL runs where reward hacking was disincentivized
reader_labels.reason: The no-hacking baselines remained low on the core evaluations, rather than developing the broad increases seen in hacking runs (r07-r12, r19-r24).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Framing hacking as acceptable or intended reduced the misalignment score by 75-90% despite reward-hacking rates over 99% (r27).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SDF inoculation and standard chat-like RLHF
reader_labels.reason: Some agentic misalignment persisted after SDF inoculation, and standard chat-like RLHF left up to 70% of pre-RLHF misalignment on some evaluations (r28, r30).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that agentic or moral-dilemma prompts removed misalignment on all evaluations, with the caveat that the evaluations were not truly held out (r31).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Offline prompt rewriting followed by SFT
reader_labels.reason: Rewriting episodes to add an inoculation prompt and then training with SFT did not prevent misalignment, especially on agentic evaluations (r32).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Different SDF corpora and reduced hard-problem filtering
reader_labels.reason: The authors report misaligned generalization across corpora when hacking was learned and also without hard-problem filtering (r33-r35, r37).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Neutral corpus and 50% non-hackable environment mixture
reader_labels.reason: The neutral corpus produced a lower-magnitude effect and had higher initial misalignment; mixing in 50% non-hackable environments reduced the effect, though it persisted (r35-r36).
